parts.description: Fire component in 秋: strokes 6–9. 禾, the grain plant, stands beside 火, fire. Think of the harvest season as a memory cue.

雨.note: 雨 yǔ means “rain.” 下雨 xiàyǔ means “to rain.”
雨.memory: Picture drops under a shelter: a top line and outer frame surround a central stroke and four rain-like dots.

parts.label: 雨
parts.name: rain shape
parts.description: Picture drops under a shelter: a top line and outer frame surround a central stroke and four rain-like dots.

只.note: 只 zhǐ means “only” here. Put it before what is limited, as in 只去了兩天, “went for only two days.”
只.memory: A small 口 sits above two spreading lower strokes. Keep those strokes separate from the mouth.

parts.label: 口
parts.name: upper mouth
parts.description: Upper mouth in 只: strokes 1–3. A small 口 sits above two spreading lower strokes. Keep those strokes separate from the mouth.

parts.label: 八
parts.name: lower strokes
parts.description: Lower strokes in 只: strokes 4–5. A small 口 sits above two spreading lower strokes. Keep those strokes separate from the mouth.

父.note: 父 fù means “father.” 父母 fùmǔ combines “father” and “mother” to mean “parents.”
父.memory: Write the two short upper strokes, then the longer crossing strokes below. The lower pair spreads wider.

parts.label: 父
parts.name: crossing form
parts.description: Write the two short upper strokes, then the longer crossing strokes below. The lower pair spreads wider.

母.note: 母 mǔ means “mother.” Learn it with 父 in 父母, “parents.”
母.memory: Notice the slanting outer shape and the two inner dots crossed by a horizontal stroke. Keep both dots visible.

parts.label: 母
parts.name: enclosing form
parts.description: Notice the slanting outer shape and the two inner dots crossed by a horizontal stroke. Keep both dots visible.

停.note: 停 tíng means “stop.” 雨快要停了 means “the rain is about to stop.”
停.memory: A person 亻 stands beside 亭. Imagine someone stopping beside a pavilion as a visual memory cue.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person component
parts.description: Person component in 停: strokes 1–2. A person 亻 stands beside 亭. Imagine someone stopping beside a pavilion as a visual memory cue.

parts.label: 亭
parts.name: pavilion component
parts.description: Pavilion component in 停: strokes 3–11. A person 亻 stands beside 亭. Imagine someone stopping beside a pavilion as a visual memory cue.

example.meaning: the rain is about to stop

底.note: 底 dǐ means “bottom; end.” At the end of a month expression, 月底 means “the end of the month.”
底.memory: The roof 广 covers 氐. Remember the small final dot underneath 氏; leaving it out changes the component.

parts.label: 广
parts.name: outer roof
parts.description: Outer roof in 底: strokes 1–3. The roof 广 covers 氐. Remember the small final dot underneath 氏; leaving it out changes the component.

parts.label: 氐
parts.name: inner component
parts.description: Inner component in 底: strokes 4–8. The roof 广 covers 氐. Remember the small final dot underneath 氏; leaving it out changes the component.

葉.note: 葉 yè means “leaf; leaves.” 紅葉 hóngyè refers to red autumn leaves in this lesson.
葉.memory: Stack the grass top, 世, and 木. Plant shapes at the top and bottom help you remember leaves.

parts.label: 艹
parts.name: grass component
parts.description: Grass component in 葉: strokes 1–4. Stack the grass top, 世, and 木. Plant shapes at the top and bottom help you remember leaves.

parts.label: 世
parts.name: middle component
parts.description: Middle component in 葉: strokes 5–9. Stack the grass top, 世, and 木. Plant shapes at the top and bottom help you remember leaves.

parts.label: 木

parts.description: Tree component in 葉: strokes 10–13. Stack the grass top, 世, and 木. Plant shapes at the top and bottom help you remember leaves.

傘.note: 傘 sǎn means “umbrella.” It is useful when talking about rain and staying dry.
傘.memory: Picture an umbrella: a broad 人-shaped canopy, paired small shapes underneath, and a central handle.

parts.label: 傘
parts.name: umbrella form
parts.description: Picture an umbrella: a broad 人-shaped canopy, paired small shapes underneath, and a central handle.

颱.note: 颱 tái is used in 颱風 táifēng, “typhoon.” Write the Traditional form with 風 on the left.
颱.memory: Wind 風 beside 台: the wind component helps you recognize the weather word.

parts.label: 風
parts.name: wind component
parts.description: Wind component in 颱: strokes 1–9. Wind 風 beside 台: the wind component helps you recognize the weather word.

parts.label: 台
parts.name: right component
parts.description: Right component in 颱: strokes 10–14. Wind 風 beside 台: the wind component helps you recognize the weather word.

濕.note: 濕 shī means “wet.” 濕濕的 describes something as wet or damp.
濕.memory: Water 氵 is on the left. On the right, 日 sits over two small thread-like forms and four bottom dots.

parts.label: 氵
parts.name: water component
parts.description: Water component in 濕: strokes 1–3. Water 氵 is on the left. On the right, 日 sits over two small thread-like forms and four bottom dots.

parts.label: 㬎
parts.name: right component
parts.description: Right component in 濕: strokes 4–17. Water 氵 is on the left. On the right, 日 sits over two small thread-like forms and four bottom dots.

討.note: 討 is the first character of 討厭 tǎoyàn, “annoying; to dislike.” Learn the combined word rather than translating each character.
討.memory: Speech 言 on the left and 寸 on the right: keep the seven speech strokes narrow.

parts.label: 言
parts.name: speech component
parts.description: Speech component in 討: strokes 1–7. Speech 言 on the left and 寸 on the right: keep the seven speech strokes narrow.

parts.label: 寸
parts.name: right component
parts.description: Right component in 討: strokes 8–10. Speech 言 on the left and 寸 on the right: keep the seven speech strokes narrow.

厭.note: 厭 is the second character of 討厭 tǎoyàn. 真討厭 can express “How annoying!”
厭.memory: The sloping 厂 shelters an inner block with two stacked boxes and 犬 alongside.

parts.label: 厂
parts.name: outer frame
parts.description: Outer frame in 厭: strokes 1–2. The sloping 厂 shelters an inner block with two stacked boxes and 犬 alongside.

parts.label: 猒
parts.name: inner component
parts.description: Inner component in 厭: strokes 3–14. The sloping 厂 shelters an inner block with two stacked boxes and 犬 alongside.

聞.note: 聞 relates to hearing. 新聞 xīnwén means “news,” not simply “new hearing.”
聞.memory: An ear 耳 inside a gate 門 is a useful image for hearing news through a doorway.

parts.label: 門
parts.name: gate component
parts.description: Gate component in 聞: strokes 1–8. An ear 耳 inside a gate 門 is a useful image for hearing news through a doorway.

parts.label: 耳
parts.name: ear component
parts.description: Ear component in 聞: strokes 9–14. An ear 耳 inside a gate 門 is a useful image for hearing news through a doorway.

更.note: 更 gèng means “even more” in comparisons. 更大 means “even bigger”; 更小 means “even smaller.”
更.memory: Keep the top line and flat box above the two long crossing strokes. The final stroke sweeps down to the right.

parts.label: 更
parts.name: crossing form
parts.description: Keep the top line and flat box above the two long crossing strokes. The final stroke sweeps down to the right.

醫.note: Medical care; learn 醫 in 醫生 yīshēng, “doctor.” The upper section has two blocks, with 酉 underneath.
醫.memory: Think of a doctor’s equipment on a shelf: two upper blocks above the wide 酉 base. Write the upper left, upper right, then the base.

parts.label: 医
parts.name: upper-left block
parts.description: The seven-stroke upper-left block encloses 矢; its final enclosing stroke comes after the inner strokes.

parts.label: 殳
parts.name: upper-right block
parts.description: Write this compact four-stroke block beside 医, above the base.

parts.label: 酉
parts.name: bottom block
parts.description: The broad seven-stroke 酉 supports both upper blocks.

直.note: 直 means “straight.” In 一直 yìzhí, it contributes the idea of continuing without a break.
直.memory: Stack the top cross above the narrow middle, then finish with the long bottom stroke. Picture a straight, continuous route.

parts.label: 十
parts.name: top cross
parts.description: The first horizontal and vertical cross above the middle.

parts.label: 目
parts.name: middle box
parts.description: Keep the five-stroke middle narrow and its horizontal lines evenly spaced.

parts.label: 一
parts.name: bottom stroke
parts.description: The final horizontal extends underneath the middle.

流.note: 流 means “to flow.” In 流鼻水 liú bíshuǐ, nasal mucus is flowing: “have a runny nose.”
流.memory: The three water strokes on the left remind you of flowing liquid; the right side ends in three descending strokes.

parts.label: 氵
parts.name: water component
parts.description: The narrow three-stroke water component goes on the left.

parts.label: 㐬
parts.name: right component
parts.description: Write the upper strokes before the three descending strokes below.

鼻.note: 鼻 means “nose.” 鼻水 bíshuǐ is nasal mucus; 流鼻水 means “have a runny nose.”
鼻.memory: Remember three stacked levels: 自, then 田, then the small base. Keep the levels centered.

parts.label: 自
parts.name: upper component
parts.description: The six-stroke 自 shape occupies the top.

parts.label: 田
parts.name: middle component
parts.description: The five-stroke 田 sits directly below 自.

parts.label: 丌
parts.name: bottom component
parts.description: Finish with the horizontal and two descending strokes beneath 田.

痛.note: 痛 means “to hurt; painful.” A body part can come before it: 頭很痛 tóu hěn tòng means “the head hurts.”
痛.memory: Use the illness frame 疒 around 甬. The frame links this shape with pain and illness.

parts.label: 疒
parts.name: illness frame
parts.description: These five strokes form the top and left frame; the two left strokes belong to the frame.

parts.label: 甬
parts.name: inner component
parts.description: Write the seven-stroke inner component inside the open frame.

胃.note: 胃 means “stomach,” the organ. 胃口 wèikǒu means “appetite,” rather than a literal “stomach mouth.”
胃.memory: A compact 田 sits above the flesh component 月. Keep the two blocks stacked, not side by side.

parts.label: 田
parts.name: upper block
parts.description: The five strokes of 田 form the upper block.

parts.label: 月
parts.name: flesh component
parts.description: This 月-shaped lower component is associated with the body here.

喉.note: 喉 is the first syllable of 喉嚨 hóulóng, “throat.” Learn and say the two-character word together.
喉.memory: A small mouth 口 sits to the left of the taller 侯. Both characters in 喉嚨 have a mouth component.

parts.label: 口
parts.name: mouth component
parts.description: Keep the three-stroke mouth small on the left.

parts.label: 侯
parts.name: right component
parts.description: The nine-stroke 侯 is the larger right-hand block; it also cues the sound hóu.

嚨.note: 嚨 is the second syllable of 喉嚨 hóulóng, “throat.” It normally appears here as part of the whole word.
嚨.memory: Remember mouth 口 beside the detailed 龍 shape. Leave most of the width for the right-hand component.

parts.label: 口
parts.name: mouth component
parts.description: Write the small mouth on the left first.

parts.label: 龍
parts.name: dragon component
parts.description: The sixteen-stroke 龍 provides the sound cue lóng; keep its internal strokes distinct.

發.note: 發 has several meanings. Here it means developing a condition: 發炎 fāyán, “be inflamed,” and 發燒 fāshāo, “have a fever.”
發.memory: Think of a roof-like top over two lower blocks: the bent 弓 on the left and 殳 on the right.

parts.label: 癶
parts.name: upper component
parts.description: These five spreading strokes form the top of 發.

parts.label: 弓
parts.name: lower-left component
parts.description: The three bent strokes form the lower-left block.

parts.label: 殳
parts.name: lower-right component
parts.description: Finish the four-stroke block on the lower right.

炎.note: 炎 relates to inflammation here. Learn 發炎 fāyán as “to be inflamed,” as in 喉嚨發炎, “the throat is inflamed.”
炎.memory: Two 火 shapes are stacked: heat above heat. Use that image to remember inflammation.

parts.label: 火
parts.name: upper fire
parts.description: The first four strokes form the smaller upper 火.

parts.label: 火
parts.name: lower fire
parts.description: The second 火 sits below and spreads wider to support the top.

病.note: 病 means “illness; sick.” 生病 shēngbìng means “fall ill / be sick.”
病.memory: The illness frame 疒 surrounds 丙. Keep the frame open on the right and bottom.

parts.label: 疒
parts.name: illness frame
parts.description: Write the five-stroke top-and-left frame first.

parts.label: 丙
parts.name: inner component
parts.description: The five-stroke 丙 sits inside; it provides a sound cue for bìng.

燒.meaning: burn; have a fever in 發燒
燒.note: 燒 means “to burn.” In 發燒 fāshāo, the whole word means “have a fever.”
燒.memory: Fire 火 stands on the left; the tall 堯 block stands on the right. The fire is your cue for burning and fever.

parts.label: 火
parts.name: fire component
parts.description: The four-stroke 火 narrows to fit the left side.

parts.label: 堯
parts.name: right component
parts.description: Keep the repeated 土 shapes above the final lower strokes.

感.note: 感 relates to feeling. 感冒 gǎnmào is the complete word for “catch/have a cold.”
感.memory: The heart 心 sits below 咸: connect the heart shape with feeling, while learning 感冒 as one word.

parts.label: 咸
parts.name: upper component
parts.description: This nine-stroke block sits above the heart.

parts.label: 心
parts.name: heart component
parts.description: The four heart strokes form a broad lower base.

冒.meaning: part of 感冒, catch/have a cold
冒.note: 冒 is the second character in 感冒 gǎnmào, “catch/have a cold.” Do not translate its parts separately to guess the word.
冒.memory: Stack a short upper box above the taller 目. Notice the different heights of the two blocks.

parts.label: 冃
parts.name: upper component
parts.description: Write the short four-stroke upper block first.

parts.label: 目
parts.name: lower component
parts.description: The five-stroke 目 is taller and sits directly below.

藥.note: 藥 yào means “medicine.” 吃藥 means “take medicine”; Chinese uses 吃, “eat,” for taking medicine.
藥.memory: A grass top 艹 sits over 樂. Picture medicinal plants above the dense lower block.

parts.label: 艹
parts.name: grass component
parts.description: This Taiwan Traditional stroke order uses four strokes for the grass top.

parts.label: 樂
parts.name: lower component
parts.description: Keep the central 白 and the side forms above the 木 at the bottom.

局.note: 局 jú appears in 藥局 yàojú, “pharmacy.” Learn the place name as a whole word.
局.memory: The upper 尸 bends over an inner 口; keep the mouth tucked inside the outer shape.

parts.label: 尸
parts.name: upper frame
parts.description: The first three strokes form the upper and left frame.

parts.label: 𠃌
parts.name: outer bend
parts.description: This bent stroke extends the frame around the inner mouth.

parts.label: 口
parts.name: inner mouth
parts.description: Finish with the three strokes of the small inner 口.

拿.note: 拿 ná means “take; hold; get.” In 拿藥 ná yào, it means to get or collect medicine.
拿.memory: 合 sits over 手: imagine a hand reaching up to take something.

parts.label: 合
parts.name: upper component
parts.description: The six strokes form 合 above the hand.

parts.label: 手
parts.name: hand component
parts.description: The four-stroke 手 sits underneath and cues taking or holding.

把.note: 把 bǎ places the affected object before the action: 把藥吃了 means “take the medicine.” It is not translated as a separate English word here.
把.memory: Remember the hand 扌 on the left and 巴 on the right. Learn the grammar separately from this visual cue.

parts.label: 扌
parts.name: hand component
parts.description: Write the three narrow hand strokes on the left.

parts.label: 巴
parts.name: right component
parts.description: The four-stroke 巴 occupies the right side and cues the sound bǎ.

休.note: 休 appears in 休息 xiūxí, “to rest.” Use the whole word when telling someone to rest.
休.memory: A person 亻 beside a tree 木 makes a useful picture of someone resting in the shade.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person component
parts.description: The two-stroke standing person is on the left.

parts.label: 木
parts.name: tree component
parts.description: The four-stroke tree fills the right side.

息.note: 息 is the second character in 休息 xiūxí, “to rest.” It also relates to breathing and resting in other words.
息.memory: 自 sits above 心. Picture settling your breathing and heart as you rest.

parts.label: 自
parts.name: upper component
parts.description: Write the six-stroke 自 above the heart.

parts.label: 心
parts.name: heart component
parts.description: The four-stroke 心 spreads below the upper block.

睡.note: 睡 shuì means “to sleep.” 睡覺 shuìjiào is the fuller word used for sleeping.
睡.memory: The eye 目 is on the left: connect it with closing your eyes to sleep. 垂 fills the right side.

parts.label: 目
parts.name: eye component
parts.description: Keep the five-stroke eye tall and narrow.

parts.label: 垂
parts.name: right component
parts.description: The eight-stroke 垂 has several crossing horizontal lines; keep them evenly spaced.

臉.note: 臉 means “face.” 臉色 liǎnsè is someone’s facial color or complexion, which can show how they feel.
臉.memory: The flesh component 月 is on the left and the wider 僉 is on the right. A face is part of the body.

parts.label: 月
parts.name: flesh component
parts.description: This four-stroke 月-shaped component relates to the body.

parts.label: 僉
parts.name: right component
parts.description: Keep the paired lower shapes under the broad top of 僉.

肚.note: 肚 appears in 肚子 dùzi, “belly; abdomen.” The 子 syllable is neutral-tone zi in this word.
肚.memory: Put flesh 月 next to 土. The body component helps distinguish 肚 from the mouth character 吐.

parts.label: 月
parts.name: flesh component
parts.description: The four-stroke body component sits on the left.

parts.label: 土
parts.name: earth component
parts.description: The three-stroke 土 sits on the right.

吐.note: 吐 is tù, fourth tone, when it means “vomit.” Learn this reading in the illness context.
吐.memory: Mouth 口 plus 土: remember something coming out of the mouth. Compare 肚, which has 月 instead.

parts.label: 口
parts.name: mouth component
parts.description: The small mouth is on the left.

parts.label: 土
parts.name: earth component
parts.description: Write the three-stroke 土 on the right.

陪.note: 陪 péi means “accompany; go or stay with someone.” 陪你去看病 means “go with you to see a doctor.”
陪.memory: The narrow 阝 stands beside 咅. Keep the left side slim so the right-hand 立-over-口 shape has room.

parts.label: 阝
parts.name: left component
parts.description: The left-side 阝 uses two strokes in this dataset.

parts.label: 咅
parts.name: right component
parts.description: Write 立 above 口 to form the right-hand block.

example.meaning: accompany you to see a doctor

健.note: 健 is the first character in 健康 jiànkāng, “health; healthy.” Learn both syllables together.
健.memory: A person 亻 stands beside 建. The person component is a useful cue for a healthy person.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person component
parts.description: The standing person occupies the left edge.

parts.label: 建
parts.name: right component
parts.description: The eight-stroke 建 fills the right side; its final sweeping stroke runs underneath.

康.note: 康 is the second character in 健康 jiànkāng, “health; healthy.” 健康中心 means “health center.”
康.memory: A broad 广 roof covers the inner strokes. Keep the central vertical visible and the lower strokes balanced.

parts.label: 广
parts.name: outer roof
parts.description: The first three strokes form the roof and left side.

parts.label: 康內部
parts.name: inner strokes
parts.description: Write the eight inner strokes beneath 广, leaving room for the lower spreading strokes.

保.note: 保 means “protect; preserve.” In 保險 bǎoxiǎn, the whole word means “insurance.”
保.memory: A person 亻 stands beside 呆, a 口 over 木. Use the image of a person protecting something as a memory cue.

parts.label: 亻
parts.name: person component
parts.description: Write the two person strokes on the left.

parts.label: 呆
parts.name: right component
parts.description: The three-stroke 口 sits above the four-stroke 木.

險.note: 險 means “danger; risk.” In 保險 bǎoxiǎn, learn the combined meaning “insurance.”
險.memory: The narrow 阝 stands beside 僉. Compare 臉: the right component is shared, but the left component changes.

parts.label: 阝
parts.name: left component
parts.description: This left-side 阝 uses two strokes.

parts.label: 僉
parts.name: right component
parts.description: The thirteen-stroke right side matches the right side of 臉.

冰.note: 冰 means “ice,” and describes something icy or ice-cold here. 冰的東西 refers to cold or icy things to eat or drink.
冰.memory: Two ice strokes 冫 beside 水: picture water turning icy. The left has two strokes, not the three of 氵.

parts.label: 冫
parts.name: ice component
parts.description: Write the dot and rising stroke on the left.

parts.label: 水
parts.name: water component
parts.description: The four-stroke 水 occupies the right side.

迷.note: In 迷路, 迷 describes losing your sense of the route.
迷.memory: Write 米 first, then let the four strokes of 辶 carry 米 along a wandering path.

parts.label: 米
parts.name: rice shape
parts.description: In 迷, write 米 (rice shape) as the first 6 strokes; Write 米 first, then let the four strokes of 辶 carry 米 along a wandering path.

parts.label: 辶
parts.name: walking radical
parts.description: In 迷, write 辶 (walking radical) as the following 4 strokes; Write 米 first, then let the four strokes of 辶 carry 米 along a wandering path.

轉.note: In 左轉 and 右轉, 轉 is a change of direction.
轉.memory: A 車 on the left turns when the right-side 專 completes the character.

parts.label: 車
parts.name: vehicle
parts.description: In 轉, write 車 (vehicle) as the first 7 strokes; A 車 on the left turns when the right-side 專 completes the character.

parts.label: 專
parts.name: right-side sound component
parts.description: In 轉, write 專 (right-side sound component) as the following 11 strokes; A 車 on the left turns when the right-side 專 completes the character.

平.note: 平 is part of 和平, the road name Heping.
平.memory: Write the top line and two short slanting strokes, then the lower horizontal and finally the central vertical.

parts.label: 一
parts.name: top line
parts.description: In 平, this top line uses strokes 1. Write the top line and two short slanting strokes, then the lower horizontal and finally the central vertical.

parts.label: 丷
parts.name: two dots
parts.description: In 平, this two dots uses strokes 2, 3. Write the top line and two short slanting strokes, then the lower horizontal and finally the central vertical.

parts.label: 十
parts.name: lower crossing strokes
parts.description: In 平, this lower crossing strokes uses strokes 4, 5. Write the top line and two short slanting strokes, then the lower horizontal and finally the central vertical.

段.note: A road can have a numbered 段, such as 一段.
段.memory: The left five strokes give the segment shape; 殳 completes the right side.

parts.label: left side
parts.name: section body
parts.description: In 段, write left side (section body) as the first 5 strokes; The left five strokes give the segment shape; 殳 completes the right side.

parts.label: 殳
parts.name: right-side component
parts.description: In 段, write 殳 (right-side component) as the following 4 strokes; The left five strokes give the segment shape; 殳 completes the right side.

綠.note: 綠 marks green in 紅綠燈.
綠.memory: The six strokes of 糹 stand on the left; finish the eight-stroke 彔 on the right.

parts.label: 糹
parts.name: silk radical
parts.description: In 綠, write 糹 (silk radical) as the first 6 strokes; The six strokes of 糹 stand on the left; finish the eight-stroke 彔 on the right.

parts.label: 彔
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 綠, write 彔 (right component) as the following 8 strokes; The six strokes of 糹 stand on the left; finish the eight-stroke 彔 on the right.

燈.note: 燈 is the lamp/light in 紅綠燈.
燈.memory: Start with four-stroke 火 on the left and write 登 on the right.

parts.label: 火
parts.name: fire radical
parts.description: In 燈, write 火 (fire radical) as the first 4 strokes; Start with four-stroke 火 on the left and write 登 on the right.

parts.label: 登
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 燈, write 登 (right component) as the following 12 strokes; Start with four-stroke 火 on the left and write 登 on the right.

第.note: 第 stands before the number in 第二, “second.”
第.memory: A six-stroke 竹 top sits above the five-stroke lower portion.

parts.name: bamboo top
parts.description: In 第, write ⺮ (bamboo top) as the first 6 strokes; A six-stroke 竹 top sits above the five-stroke lower portion.

parts.label: lower portion
parts.name: ordinal base
parts.description: In 第, write lower portion (ordinal base) as the following 5 strokes; A six-stroke 竹 top sits above the five-stroke lower portion.

告.note: 告 is the first syllable of 告訴, “tell.”
告.memory: Four strokes at the top stand over the three-stroke mouth 口: telling uses the mouth.

parts.label: upper element
parts.name: top of 告
parts.description: In 告, write upper element (top of 告) as the first 4 strokes; Four strokes at the top stand over the three-stroke mouth 口: telling uses the mouth.

parts.label: 口
parts.name: mouth
parts.description: In 告, write 口 (mouth) as the following 3 strokes; Four strokes at the top stand over the three-stroke mouth 口: telling uses the mouth.

訴.memory: Seven strokes of 言 occupy the left and five strokes of 斥 occupy the right.

parts.label: 言
parts.name: speech
parts.description: In 訴, write 言 (speech) as the first 7 strokes; Seven strokes of 言 occupy the left and five strokes of 斥 occupy the right.

parts.label: 斥
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 訴, write 斥 (right component) as the following 5 strokes; Seven strokes of 言 occupy the left and five strokes of 斥 occupy the right.

提.note: 提 is the action in 提錢, withdrawing cash.
提.memory: The three-stroke hand 扌 lifts the nine-stroke 是 at the right.

parts.label: 扌
parts.name: hand radical
parts.description: In 提, write 扌 (hand radical) as the first 3 strokes; The three-stroke hand 扌 lifts the nine-stroke 是 at the right.

parts.label: 是
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 提, write 是 (right component) as the following 9 strokes; The three-stroke hand 扌 lifts the nine-stroke 是 at the right.

款.note: 款 refers to funds in 提款機.
款.memory: Keep the left block compact; the four-stroke 欠 stands clearly to its right.

parts.label: left block
parts.name: funds component
parts.description: In 款, write left block (funds component) as the first 8 strokes; Keep the left block compact; the four-stroke 欠 stands clearly to its right.

parts.label: 欠
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 款, write 欠 (right component) as the following 4 strokes; Keep the left block compact; the four-stroke 欠 stands clearly to its right.

郵.note: 郵 gives 郵局 its postal meaning.
郵.memory: The nine-stroke 垂 is to the left of three-stroke 阝, the place-related side.

parts.label: 垂
parts.name: left component
parts.description: In 郵, write 垂 (left component) as the first 9 strokes; The nine-stroke 垂 is to the left of three-stroke 阝, the place-related side.

parts.label: 阝
parts.name: place component
parts.description: In 郵, write 阝 (place component) as the following 3 strokes; The nine-stroke 垂 is to the left of three-stroke 阝, the place-related side.

著.note: In 看著, 著 marks an action or state continuing.
著.memory: Write the grass top 艹 before the lower 者; this word is pronounced neutral-tone zhe.

parts.label: 艹
parts.name: grass top
parts.description: In 著, write 艹 (grass top) as the first 3 strokes; Write the grass top 艹 before the lower 者; this word is pronounced neutral-tone zhe.

parts.label: 者
parts.name: lower component
parts.description: In 著, write 者 (lower component) as the following 8 strokes; Write the grass top 艹 before the lower 者; this word is pronounced neutral-tone zhe.

品.note: 品 is the goods in 日用品.
品.memory: The single 口 above two 口 below makes three mouths in a triangular arrangement.

parts.label: 口
parts.name: top mouth
parts.description: In 品, write 口 (top mouth) as the first 3 strokes; The single 口 above two 口 below makes three mouths in a triangular arrangement.

parts.label: 吅
parts.name: two lower mouths
parts.description: In 品, write 吅 (two lower mouths) as the following 6 strokes; The single 口 above two 口 below makes three mouths in a triangular arrangement.

巷.note: 巷 names the narrow lane in 巷子.
巷.memory: The six-stroke 共 sits over the three-stroke lower enclosure 己.

parts.label: 共
parts.name: upper element
parts.description: In 巷, write 共 (upper element) as the first 6 strokes; The six-stroke 共 sits over the three-stroke lower enclosure 己.

parts.label: 己
parts.name: lower enclosure
parts.description: In 巷, write 己 (lower enclosure) as the following 3 strokes; The six-stroke 共 sits over the three-stroke lower enclosure 己.

餓.note: 餓 tells how the walkers feel before eating noodles.
餓.memory: The eight-stroke 飠 food radical sits left of 我: I need food.

parts.label: 飠
parts.name: food radical
parts.description: In 餓, write 飠 (food radical) as the first 8 strokes; The eight-stroke 飠 food radical sits left of 我: I need food.

parts.label: 我
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 餓, write 我 (right component) as the following 7 strokes; The eight-stroke 飠 food radical sits left of 我: I need food.

離.note: 離 links two places in 學校離郵局很近.
離.memory: The eleven-stroke 离 is on the left; finish the bird-shaped 隹 on the right.

parts.label: 离
parts.name: left component
parts.description: In 離, write 离 (left component) as the first 11 strokes; The eleven-stroke 离 is on the left; finish the bird-shaped 隹 on the right.

parts.label: 隹
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 離, write 隹 (right component) as the following 8 strokes; The eleven-stroke 离 is on the left; finish the bird-shaped 隹 on the right.

背.note: 背包 is a backpack worn on your back.
背.memory: Five strokes of 北 sit on top of four-stroke 月.

parts.label: 北
parts.name: upper component
parts.description: In 背, write 北 (upper component) as the first 5 strokes; Five strokes of 北 sit on top of four-stroke 月.

parts.label: 月
parts.name: lower component
parts.description: In 背, write 月 (lower component) as the following 4 strokes; Five strokes of 北 sit on top of four-stroke 月.

正.note: 正好 means “just right” or “happen to.”
正.memory: One horizontal stroke sits over four-stroke 止; keep the central vertical straight.

parts.label: 一
parts.name: top line
parts.description: In 正, write 一 (top line) as the first 1 stroke; One horizontal stroke sits over four-stroke 止; keep the central vertical straight.

parts.label: 止
parts.name: lower component
parts.description: In 正, write 止 (lower component) as the following 4 strokes; One horizontal stroke sits over four-stroke 止; keep the central vertical straight.

筆.note: 筆 means pen or writing instrument. You will learn its counting word after this character.
筆.memory: The bamboo top ⺮ has six strokes, and the writing hand 聿 has six below.

parts.name: bamboo top
parts.description: In 筆, write ⺮ (bamboo top) as the first 6 strokes; The bamboo top ⺮ has six strokes, and the writing hand 聿 has six below.

parts.label: 聿
parts.name: writing component
parts.description: In 筆, write 聿 (writing component) as the following 6 strokes; The bamboo top ⺮ has six strokes, and the writing hand 聿 has six below.

枝.note: 枝 counts long thin items such as pens in 兩枝筆.
枝.memory: The four-stroke 木 is on the left and four-stroke 支 on the right.

parts.label: 木
parts.name: wood radical
parts.description: In 枝, write 木 (wood radical) as the first 4 strokes; The four-stroke 木 is on the left and four-stroke 支 on the right.

parts.label: 支
parts.name: right component
parts.description: In 枝, write 支 (right component) as the following 4 strokes; The four-stroke 木 is on the left and four-stroke 支 on the right.

u2-pronouns.title: Change the person, keep the pattern
u2-pronouns.explanation: 他 means he or him; 她 means she or her. Both sound tā. Written Mandarin distinguishes them, while speech relies on context. 是 stays the same for every person: no separate forms for am, is, and are.
u2-pronouns.remember: Use 是 for an identity such as student. Chinese does not need a word for the English article a in this sentence.

examples.meaning: He is a student.
She is a student.

u2-plurals.title: From I to we
u2-plurals.explanation: 我們 means we or us, 你們 means you when addressing more than one person, and 他們 means they or them. 們 has a light neutral tone. 他們 can refer to a male or mixed group.
u2-plurals.remember: 學生 stays the same for student and students. 們 is not a general plural ending for every noun, and you do not add it after a number + measure word.

examples.meaning: We are students.
Are you (plural) students?

u2-also.title: A small word for also
u2-also.explanation: 也 means also or too. It goes before the verb in these sentences, after the person. Use it when adding someone to something already said: you are a student; I am a student too.
u2-also.remember: Keep 也 before 是. Unlike English too, it does not go at the end of these sentences.

examples.meaning: I am a student too.
They are students too.

u2-not.title: Say that something is not true
u2-not.explanation: 不 goes before 是 to make it negative. 我不是學生 means I am not a student. If you also need 也, it comes before 不: 也不是 means is not either. The verb does not change, and there is no extra word for do or does.
u2-not.remember: 不 is bù alone, but sounds bú before a fourth tone, as in 不是 (bú shì). To answer 你是學生嗎？, use 是 (yes, I am) or 不是 (no, I am not).

examples.meaning: I am not a student.
She is not a student either.

u2-possession.title: My, your, his, her
u2-possession.explanation: 的 links the person to the noun that follows. 我的學生 means my student; 你的學生 means your student. 他的 and 她的 mean his and her. The noun comes last, just as it does in the English phrase my student.
u2-possession.remember: 的 is light-toned de here. It can describe a relationship, such as a teacher and student, not just ownership. To make a full identity sentence, add the person + 是 before this noun phrase.

examples.meaning: my student
She is my student.

u2-counting.title: Count one person
u2-counting.explanation: 一 means one; 人 means person or people. When counting people in everyday speech, put 個 between the number and the noun: 一個人. 個 is a measure word (also called a classifier). It is common with people and many things, but other nouns need other measure words, which we will introduce when needed.
u2-counting.remember: 一 is yī alone. Before the fourth-tone word 個 (gè), it becomes yí. 個 often sounds light: yí ge. Do not add 們 to a counted noun. 我是學生 still works without 一個 when simply giving an identity.

examples.meaning: one person
one student

u2-have.title: Have, or there is
u2-have.pattern: person + 有 + noun phrase / 有 + noun phrase
u2-have.explanation: 有 means have when a person comes before it. Imagine a tutor talking about a student: 她有一個學生 = she has one student. With no possessor before 有, it can mean there is or there are. 有 is already the verb; do not add 是 before it.
u2-have.remember: 一個學生 and 一個人 are the number + measure word + noun pattern you just learned.

examples.meaning: She has one student.
There is one person.

u2-no-have.title: The special negative of 有
u2-no-have.pattern: person + 沒有 + noun / 沒有 + noun
u2-no-have.explanation: Use 沒有 to say do not have or there is not / there are no. 有 takes 沒 instead of 不: say 沒有, never 不有. Without a number, a Chinese noun can be singular or plural; context supplies that information.
u2-no-have.remember: Keep the useful pair together: 有 ↔ 沒有. With 是, the negative is still 不是.

examples.meaning: I do not have any students.
There is nobody.

u2-have-question.title: Ask about having something
u2-have-question.explanation: The question rule from Unit 1 still works: add 嗎 to a statement. Keep the normal word order. To answer briefly, repeat the verb 有 for yes, or its negative 沒有 for no.
u2-have-question.remember: Answer this 有 question with 有 or 沒有. Use 是 or 不是 when answering an identity question with 是.

examples.meaning: Do you have any students?
Yes, I do. / No, I do not.

u3-point.title: Point to this or that
u3-point.pattern: 這 / 那 + measure word + noun
u3-point.explanation: 這 means this, nearby; 那 means that, farther away. When naming this person or that student, put the measure word 個 between 這 or 那 and the noun. This is the same 個 you used when counting people. 這 and 那 can also stand alone as this and that.
u3-point.remember: Use 這個人, not 這人, in the full beginner pattern here. To make a sentence, the whole phrase 這個人 can be the subject before 是.

examples.meaning: this person
That person is a student.

u3-what.title: Ask what something is
u3-what.pattern: 這 / 那 + 是 + 什麼？
u3-what.explanation: 什麼 is one word meaning what. Keep it in the position of the information you want: 這是書 (this is a book) becomes 這是什麼 (what is this). Do not move what to the front as English does. 書 means book or books; the noun itself does not change.
u3-what.remember: An information question with 什麼 does not need 嗎. 那是書嗎？ asks is that a book? and expects yes or no. 這 stands alone in 這是書, so no measure word is needed between 這 and 是.

examples.meaning: What is this?
This is a book.

u3-books.title: A measure word for books
u3-books.pattern: number + 本 + 書 / 這 or 那 + 本 + 書
u3-books.explanation: You already know number + measure word + noun. For books, use 本 in the measure-word slot: 一本書 means one book. Use 本 with 這 and 那 too: 這本書 means this book; 那本書 means that book. The noun tells you which measure word fits.
u3-books.remember: Use 本 for books here, and 個 for people or students. 一 sounds yì before a first, second, or third tone, so 一本 is yì běn. Before a fourth tone it sounds yí, as in 一個 (yí ge). Alone, it is yī.

examples.meaning: one book
that book

u3-two.title: Two books, two people
u3-two.explanation: Use 兩 for two before a measure word when counting things or people: 兩本書 (two books), 兩個人 (two people). Keep the same measure word you would use for one. No plural ending is added to 書 or 人.
u3-two.remember: Mandarin also has 二 (èr), used when counting aloud or reading digits. We will practice that later; use 兩 before 本 and 個 here. In 兩本, the first third tone changes in speech, just like 你好; the pinyin keeps dictionary tones.

examples.meaning: two books
I have two books.

u3-adjectives.title: Describe something as big or small
u3-adjectives.explanation: 大 means big and 小 means small. A simple positive description uses 很 before the adjective: 這本書很大. Do not insert 是: an adjective can do the describing without it. 很 can mean very, but in a neutral description like this it often just links the subject to the adjective, without strong emphasis.
u3-adjectives.remember: Compare an identity, 這是書 (this is a book), with a description, 這本書很大 (this book is big). Do not translate every English is as 是.

examples.meaning: This book is big.
That book is small.

u3-not-size.title: Say it is not big
u3-not-size.explanation: For a simple negative description, put 不 directly before the adjective. 這本書不大 means this book is not big. You do not need 是 or 很 in this pattern. 不大 does not automatically mean small; it only denies that something is big.
u3-not-size.remember: 不 sounds bú before the fourth tone of 大, but stays bù before 小. This is the same tone rule you met in 不是.

examples.meaning: This book is not big.
That book is not small.

u3-location.title: Say where someone or something is
u3-location.explanation: 在 means be at or in a place here. 這裡 means here, and 那裡 means there: learn each as a whole place word. 我在這裡 means I am here. Put the person or thing first, then 在, then the place. 在 is already the verb in this pattern; no 是 is needed.
u3-location.remember: 有 introduces something that exists: 有一本書 (there is a book). 在 gives the location of something: 這本書在這裡 (this book is here). 裡 is the Traditional form used in our Taiwan writing practice.

examples.meaning: I am here.
My book is there.

u3-location-question.title: Is it here?
u3-location-question.pattern: person or thing + 在 + place + 嗎？
u3-location-question.explanation: Reuse your yes/no question rule: add 嗎 to a location statement without changing the word order. To answer briefly, repeat 在 for yes, or 不在 for no. 在 takes 不 for a negative, unlike 有, which takes 沒.
u3-location-question.remember: Match the answer to the verb in the question: 在 / 不在 for location, 有 / 沒有 for having, 是 / 不是 for identity. 不在 sounds bú zài before the fourth tone.

examples.pinyin: nǐ de shū zài nàlǐ ma?
examples.meaning: Is your book there?
Yes, it is. / No, it is not.

u3-all.title: Everyone in the group
u3-all.explanation: 都 means all, or both when the group has two members. It refers to the group before it: 我們都在這裡 means we are all here. Place 都 after that group and before 在 or 是. You can use a counted group too: 兩個學生都在那裡.
u3-all.remember: The order is 我們 + 都 + 在 + 這裡. 都 does not go at the end like too sometimes does in English. Here it is pronounced dōu.

examples.meaning: We are all here.
They are all students.

u4-movement.title: Going somewhere, coming here
u4-movement.explanation: 去 means go, away from the speaker or the place treated as the reference point. 來 means come, toward that reference point. The destination follows the verb directly: 去那裡 (go there), 來這裡 (come here). You do not need an extra word for the English to.
u4-movement.remember: 在 gives a location: 我在這裡 (I am here). 來 and 去 describe movement. The verb stays the same for different people; do not add 是 before it.

examples.meaning: I go there.
He comes here.

u4-where.title: Ask where
u4-where.pattern: person + 在 / 去 + 哪裡？
u4-where.explanation: 哪裡 means where. Like 什麼, it stays in the position of the missing information. 你在這裡 (you are here) becomes 你在哪裡 (where are you). With 去, replace the destination instead: 你去哪裡 means where are you going.
u4-where.remember: Do not add 嗎 to this information question. Compare 哪裡 (nǎlǐ, where) and 那裡 (nàlǐ, there): a component and a tone make the difference. As in 你好, the first third tone of 哪裡 changes in speech; the pinyin keeps dictionary tones.

examples.meaning: Where are you?
Where are you going?

u4-actions.title: Say what someone does
u4-actions.explanation: An action verb can go directly after the person, followed by its object: 我看書 means I read books. 看 can mean look, watch, or read; with 書 it means read. There is no 是 before the action and no verb ending for he, she, or they. 書 without a number can refer to books generally.
u4-actions.remember: For an ordinary negative here, put 不 before the action: 不看. This does not mean did not read; past-event negatives come later. Add 嗎 for yes/no, or keep 什麼 in the object slot to ask what: 你看什麼？

examples.meaning: I read books.
He does not read books.

u4-and.title: Join two people or things
u4-and.explanation: 和 means and when joining people or things. 他和她 means he and she. The combined phrase can be the subject; put 都 after the whole group to say both of them: 他和她都看書. The same joining pattern works with things, such as this book and that book.
u4-and.remember: Use 和 to join nouns here, not as a general link between complete sentences or separate actions. We show hé in pinyin; hàn is also used for and in Taiwan.

examples.pinyin: tā hé tā dōu shì xuéshēng
examples.meaning: He and she are both students.

examples.pinyin: zhè běn shū hé nà běn shū
examples.meaning: this book and that book

u4-languages.title: Learn a language
u4-languages.explanation: 中文 means Chinese, and 英文 means English. In our lessons, speaking 中文 means speaking Mandarin. Both names end in 文. You already wrote 學 inside 學生; now use 學 as a word on its own: learn or study. Put the language after it: 我學中文.
u4-languages.remember: 中文 and 英文 are language names, not identities for people. No measure word is needed when saying which language you study. 學生 is one word, student; 學 is now a separate verb, learn or study.

examples.meaning: I study Chinese.
She studies Chinese and English.

u4-speech.title: Speaking and listening
u4-speech.explanation: 說 means speak or say; 聽 means listen or listen to. To name a language, put it directly after the verb: 說中文, 聽英文. English uses to in listen to English, but Mandarin does not add a separate word for it in this pattern.
u4-speech.remember: 聽 says that you listen; it does not by itself say that you understand. Keep the action + object order from 看書 and 學中文.

examples.meaning: I speak English.
I listen to Chinese.

u4-wish.title: Say what you would like to do
u4-wish.explanation: Before an action, 想 can mean want to or would like to. It comes between the person and the action: 我想看書. There is no extra word for English to. You can use the same pattern with an action and a place, such as 想去那裡.
u4-wish.remember: Use 想 + an action for want to here. 想 has other meanings, including think about or miss; it is not a general replacement for want directly before a thing.

examples.meaning: I want to read.
I want to learn Chinese.

u4-intention.title: Want something, or intend to act
u4-intention.explanation: 要 can be followed by something you want: 我要這本書 (I want this book). It can also come before an action to express a more definite intention: 我要學中文 (I intend to study Chinese). 想 often sounds more like a wish; 要 often sounds more decided. Context still matters.
u4-intention.remember: Compare 想看書 (want to read) with 要這本書 (want this book). We are practicing desire and intention here; 要 is not an automatic translation of every English future tense.

examples.meaning: I want this book.
I intend to study Chinese.

u4-negative-wish.title: Say what you do not want
u4-negative-wish.pattern: person + 不 + 想 / 要 + rest
u4-negative-wish.explanation: To deny the wish itself, put 不 before 想 or 要. 我不想去 means I do not want to go. 我不要這本書 means I do not want this book. In 不想去, the negative belongs before want, not between want and go.
u4-negative-wish.remember: 不想 keeps bù before the third tone; 不要 sounds bú yào before the fourth tone. 不要 can also tell someone not to do something, but these examples are statements about what I want, not commands.

examples.meaning: I do not want to go.

examples.pinyin: wǒ bú yào zhè běn shū
examples.meaning: I do not want this book.

u4-ability.title: Say what you know how to do
u4-ability.explanation: Use 會 before an action for a learned skill: 我會說英文 means I know how to speak English. Put 不 before 會 for do not know how to: 我不會說中文. Add 嗎 to ask a yes/no question, and answer briefly with 會 or 不會.
u4-ability.remember: 不說 means do not speak, 不想說 means do not want to speak, and 不會說 means do not know how to speak. This use of 會 is about skill, not permission. Its other uses, including predictions, come later.

examples.meaning: Can you speak English?
I do not know how to speak Chinese.

u5-drink.title: Talk about a drink
u5-drink.explanation: 喝 works like 看 and 聽: put the thing after the action. 茶 names tea generally; no measure word is needed when saying what you drink.
u5-drink.remember: 不 goes before 喝. Do not add 是 before an action.

examples.meaning: I drink tea.
She does not drink tea.

u5-taste.title: Say a drink tastes good
u5-taste.explanation: 好喝 means pleasant to drink. Treat it as a describing word, like 大 and 小. 很 connects the subject and the description in a neutral statement; stronger stress can make it mean very.
u5-taste.remember: Use 好喝 for drinks. You already know 好, but learn 好喝 as a whole expression. No 是 is needed.

examples.meaning: The tea tastes good.
This tastes good.

u5-please.title: Offer something politely
u5-please.explanation: Place 請 before an action when inviting someone to do it politely. With a drink, this is a way to offer it to your guest. The person you address is often left unstated.
u5-please.remember: 請 introduces the invitation; it is not a question particle and does not go at the end.

examples.meaning: Please have some tea.
Please look at this book.

u5-likes.title: Say what you like
u5-likes.explanation: 喜歡 means like. It can be followed by a thing or by an action phrase. Put 不 before the entire word to say dislike or do not like.
u5-likes.remember: 喜歡 is a preference; 想 is a wish to do something. 喜歡喝茶 says you enjoy drinking tea, not that you want tea right now.

examples.meaning: I like reading.
She does not like tea.

u5-coffee.title: Tea and coffee
u5-coffee.explanation: 咖啡 is coffee, a two-character borrowed word. Both syllables have the first tone. Use the same action and preference patterns with this new drink.
u5-coffee.remember: 咖 and 啡 are character parts of one vocabulary word; do not translate them separately.

examples.meaning: She drinks coffee.
I do not like coffee.

u5-a-not-a.title: Ask with an action and its negative
u5-a-not-a.explanation: You can form a yes/no question by giving the positive and negative versions of the first verb. Use 要不要 to ask about wanting, 喝不喝 about drinking, and 是不是 about identity. The object stays at the end.
u5-a-not-a.remember: Choose this structure OR a statement followed by 嗎. Do not combine them. 不 is often light in A-not-A questions; pinyin here shows neutral bu.

examples.pinyin: nǐ yào bu yào hē chá?
examples.meaning: Would you like some tea?
Is she a student?

u5-answers.title: Give a short answer
u5-answers.pattern: repeat the questioned verb / 不 + verb
u5-answers.explanation: Answer a simple yes/no question by repeating the verb that was questioned. For 要不要, use 要 or 不要. For a question about liking, use 喜歡 or 不喜歡. English yes does not always become 是.
u5-answers.remember: Use 是 or 不是 for an identity question with 是. The negative of 有 remains 沒有, as you learned earlier.

examples.pinyin: nǐ yào bu yào hē chá? yào
examples.meaning: Would you like tea? Yes.

examples.pinyin: nǐ xǐhuān kāfēi ma? bù xǐhuān
examples.meaning: Do you like coffee? No.

u5-follow-up.title: Ask “and you?”
u5-follow-up.explanation: After someone states a preference or answers a question, use another person followed by 呢 to return the same topic to them. The earlier sentence supplies what you are asking about.
u5-follow-up.remember: 呢 is light and neutral here. It needs context; it is not an interchangeable replacement for 嗎.

examples.pinyin: wǒ xǐhuān kàn shū. nǐ ne?
examples.meaning: I like reading. And you?
I drink tea. What about him?

u5-thanks.title: Say thank you
u5-thanks.explanation: 謝謝 is the common expression for thanking someone. You can add the person directly, as in 謝謝你. The second syllable is often light in everyday speech.
u5-thanks.remember: Write 謝 twice, but count 謝謝 as one expression. No 的 or 是 is needed.

examples.meaning: Thank you.
Thank you all.

u6-family.title: Meet the family
u6-family.explanation: 家 means home or family. 家人 means family members: 家 with the familiar 人. 爸爸 is dad; 媽媽 is mom. Use the familiar 這是 to introduce them. With a pronoun and a close family relationship, 的 is often left out: 我爸爸 means my dad. 我的爸爸 is also grammatical. We will practise this more later in this unit.
u6-family.remember: The second syllables in bàba and māma are light-toned. 人 is review, not a new character.

examples.meaning: This is my family.
This is my dad.
This is my mom.

u6-siblings.title: Older or younger?
u6-siblings.explanation: 哥哥 means older brother, 姐姐 older sister, and 妹妹 younger sister. The second syllable of each word is light-toned. Reuse 有 and 沒有 for have and do not have. Reuse 個 to count a sibling; use 兩 before 個 for two. 我姐姐 and 你哥哥 use the close-family pattern already introduced.
u6-siblings.remember: For two + classifier, use 兩個. A yes/no question with 有 can be answered with 有 or 沒有.

examples.meaning: I have one older brother.
I have two younger sisters.
I do not have an older sister.

u6-who.title: Ask who a person is
u6-who.explanation: 誰 (shéi) means who. Put it where the unknown person belongs. In 這是誰, the identity after 是 is unknown. In 誰是你哥哥, the person before 是 is unknown. Keep that position; do not add 嗎 to a question already using 誰.
u6-who.remember: You can answer 這是誰？ with 這是我姐姐。

examples.meaning: Who is this?
Who is your older brother?

u6-photos.title: Count and point to photos
u6-photos.explanation: 照片 (zhàopiàn) means photo. 張 (zhāng) is a measure word used for flat objects such as photographs, paper, and tables. For photos, use number + 張 + 照片. To say this photo, use the familiar pointing pattern with 張: 這張照片.
u6-photos.remember: Use 兩張 for two photos. 一 is pronounced yì before first-tone 張. Keep both fourth tones in zhàopiàn.

examples.meaning: one photo
two photos
this photo
I have two photos.

u6-whose.title: Whose photo?
u6-whose.explanation: You already know 的 for a connection or possession. 誰的 means whose: put 誰 where the person would be. Keep 照片 after 的. In 我姐姐的照片, the first connection is my sister, and the final 的 links her to the photo.
u6-whose.remember: A photo can belong to someone or show them. Context tells you which connection is meant. Here the family-photo example shows the family.

examples.meaning: Whose photo is this?

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ jiějie de zhàopiàn.
examples.meaning: This is my older sister’s photo.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ jiārén de zhàopiàn.
examples.meaning: This is a photo of my family.

u6-close.title: 我媽媽, not always 我的媽媽
u6-close.explanation: With close family relationships, Chinese often drops 的 after a pronoun: 我爸爸, 我媽媽, 我哥哥. 我家 is also natural for my home or my family. 我的爸爸 is grammatical, but 我爸爸 is very natural in ordinary conversation. This does not mean you can remove 的 everywhere: keep it in 我的照片.
u6-close.remember: Both 我媽媽 and 我的媽媽 are grammatical. Keep 的 in 我姐姐的照片 to link the sister to the photo.

examples.meaning: This is my dad.
This is my mom.
my home / my family
my photo

u7-count.title: Ask for the number
u7-count.explanation: You already know 有, 沒有, 個 and 兩. 幾 (jǐ) asks “how many” when a fairly small number is expected. Replace the number with 幾; keep 個 and the noun in place. In 你家有幾個人, 家 refers to the family/household and 人 to its members. Answer by replacing 幾 with a number you know. 幾 already makes this a question, so do not add 嗎.
u7-count.remember: Use 兩個 for two. In these counting phrases, 個 is often pronounced lightly as ge.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ ge rén?
examples.meaning: How many people are in your family?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu liǎng ge rén.
examples.meaning: There are two people in my family.

u7-photo-hobby.title: From a photo to taking photos
u7-photo-hobby.explanation: 照片 (zhàopiàn) is a thing: a photo. 照相 (zhàoxiàng) is an activity: take photos. They share 照 but have different second characters and meanings. You already know 喜歡 (xǐhuān). Put the activity directly after it to say what you like doing. Use 不喜歡 for an activity you do not like.
u7-photo-hobby.remember: 照片 is the photo; 照相 is taking it. Keep the book’s xǐhuān spelling.

examples.meaning: I like taking photos.
My older sister does not like taking photos.

u7-weekend.title: Ask what happens at the weekend
u7-weekend.explanation: 週末 (zhōumò) means weekend; 做 (zuò) means do. 做什麼 means do what. A time word normally goes after the subject and before the activity: 你週末做什麼？ It can also go before the subject: 週末你做什麼？ Both are natural. 什麼 stays where the unknown activity belongs, and you do not add 嗎.
u7-weekend.remember: Put 週末 before the activity. For the building exercises, follow the requested time-word position.

examples.meaning: What do you do at the weekend?
At the weekend, I take photos.
What do you like doing?

u7-go.title: Go and do an activity
u7-go.explanation: You know 去, go. Put a complete activity after it to say “go do that activity”: 去游泳, go swimming; 去看電影, go see a movie. Keep the activity’s own verb. Add the time before 去 to say when. This pattern can express a plan; no English-style “to” needs an extra Chinese word.
u7-go.remember: 去 tells us we go; the phrase after 去 tells us what we go to do.

examples.meaning: At the weekend, I go swimming.
We are going to see a movie.

u7-often.title: Say what you do often
u7-often.explanation: 常 (cháng) means often: an activity happens frequently. It does not mean every time, and it is not an exact equivalent of “usually.” Put 常 before the whole activity. To say what you often do on weekends, put 週末 before 常.
u7-often.remember: Time first, then 常, then the activity.

examples.meaning: I often watch movies.
I often swim on weekends.

u7-also-all.title: Old words, new activities
u7-also-all.pattern: subject + 也 / 都 + verb phrase
u7-also-all.explanation: 也 (yě), also, and 都 (dōu), all/both, are review from earlier units. Use 也 to add a matching fact in a conversation: someone likes swimming, and you do too. Use 都 with a group such as 我們 to say the statement is true of everyone in that group. Both go before 喜歡 when describing shared likes. Here 都 means all/both, not often.
u7-also-all.remember: 也 adds “too”; 都 includes everyone; 常 tells how often. Practise them separately here.

examples.text: 她喜歡游泳。我也喜歡游泳。
examples.pinyin: Tā xǐhuān yóuyǒng. Wǒ yě xǐhuān yóuyǒng.
examples.meaning: She likes swimming. I like swimming too.
We all like watching movies.

u7-suggest.title: Make a friendly suggestion
u7-suggest.pattern: 我們 + 去 + activity + 吧
u7-suggest.explanation: 吧 (ba) is a light, neutral-tone particle at the end of a sentence. After 我們去 + activity, it makes a simple suggestion: “Let’s go…” The listener can accept with the familiar 好, “OK.” You know 嗎 for a yes/no question. Here 吧 proposes something to do together; it does not ask whether a statement is true.
u7-suggest.remember: Put 吧 at the very end of the suggestion and pronounce it lightly.

examples.meaning: Let’s go see a movie.
Let’s go swimming.

u7-describe.title: People and descriptions
u7-describe.explanation: 老師 (lǎoshī) means teacher. Use 是 to identify a person’s role: 她是老師. 好看 (hǎokàn) means good-looking or nice to look at. Use 很 before this description, without 是: 這張照片很好看. You already know the two sentence patterns; the new words let you say more about people and photos.
u7-describe.remember: A role follows 是. A simple adjective description follows 很.

examples.meaning: My older sister is a teacher.
This photo looks nice.

u7-movies.title: From reading to watching movies
u7-movies.explanation: You know 看 from 看書, read a book. 看電影 (kàn diànyǐng) means watch movies: 電影 is movie, and 看 tells us what we do. Keep 看電影 together as one activity after 喜歡. 照相 means take photos; 看電影 means watch movies.
u7-movies.remember: The familiar 看 takes a different object: 書 or 電影.

examples.meaning: I like watching movies.
She does not like watching movies.

u7-swim.title: One more activity: swimming
u7-swim.explanation: 游泳 (yóuyǒng) means swim. These two characters make one activity; learn both together. You can put 游泳 straight after 喜歡 or 想. 我喜歡游泳 describes a general preference; 我想游泳 says what you want to do.
u7-swim.remember: 游 and 泳 both have a water component. Keep the whole word 游泳 together.

examples.meaning: I like swimming.
I want to swim.

u8-time.title: Today or tomorrow
u8-time.pattern: subject + 今天 / 明天 + activity
u8-time.explanation: 今天 (jīntiān) means today; 明天 (míngtiān) means tomorrow. Both share 天. Reuse the time position you learned with 週末: put 今天 or 明天 before the activity. Time can go just after the subject or at the beginning. No extra word is needed for English “on” or “will.” The building prompt tells you which subject/time order to use.
u8-time.remember: 今天 is today. 明天 is tomorrow. Both time expressions go before the action.

examples.meaning: I am going swimming tomorrow.
We are going to see a movie today.

u8-opinion.title: Say what you think about an activity
u8-opinion.pattern: person + 覺得 + activity + 很好玩
u8-opinion.explanation: 覺得 (juéde) introduces an opinion: “I think / I feel that…” 好玩 (hǎowán) means fun or enjoyable. 我覺得游泳很好玩 contains a complete idea after 覺得: 游泳很好玩, swimming is fun. The activity is what you describe. Reuse 很 before the description, without 是. 想 + action already means “want to”; 覺得 + statement tells us your opinion instead. No extra word for English “that” is needed.
u8-opinion.remember: 想游泳: want to swim. 覺得游泳很好玩: think swimming is fun.

examples.meaning: I think swimming is fun.
She thinks taking photos is fun.

u8-not-fun.title: Disagree with an opinion
u8-not-fun.explanation: 好玩 is a description, like 好看. Put 不 directly before 好玩 to say “not fun.” In this basic negative description, do not keep 很. Compare 不好玩, not fun, with 不想去, do not want to go: an opinion about the activity and a decision about going are different messages.
u8-not-fun.remember: Disagree with the description using 不好玩. Decline an activity using the familiar 不想 + action.

examples.meaning: I think taking photos is not fun.
I do not want to go take photos.

u8-together.title: Make it a shared activity
u8-together.pattern: subject + time + 一起 + 去 + activity
u8-together.explanation: 一起 (yìqǐ) means together: the people do the activity with one another. Put it before 去 or another action, not at the end as in English. 我們都去 says everyone goes; 我們一起去 says we go together. Everyone could go separately, so 都 and 一起 are not interchangeable. 一 is pronounced yì before the third tone qǐ.
u8-together.remember: Time comes before 一起; 一起 comes before the action.

examples.meaning: We are going swimming together tomorrow.
We watch movies together.

u8-invite.title: Ask how the plan sounds
u8-invite.explanation: 怎麼樣 (zěnmeyàng) asks “How does that sound?” after a proposed plan. First say what you suggest, then ask for the other person’s reaction. 好啊 (hǎo a), “Sure!” or “OK!”, accepts warmly. 啊 is a light sentence-final particle; here learn it as part of 好啊. You already know 吧 for a suggestion; 怎麼樣 explicitly asks the listener to respond. Do not add 嗎 after this question.
u8-invite.remember: Offer a concrete plan, ask 怎麼樣, then listen for acceptance or another suggestion.

examples.text: 我們明天一起去游泳，怎麼樣？
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen míngtiān yìqǐ qù yóuyǒng, zěnmeyàng?
examples.meaning: How about going swimming together tomorrow?
Sure!

u8-possible.title: Say what an activity lets you do
u8-possible.explanation: 可以 (kěyǐ) here means can in the sense of possibility. 看電影可以學中文 says watching movies can be a way to learn Chinese. The first activity is what the sentence is about; 可以 introduces what becomes possible through it. This does not say watching one movie guarantees fluency. You already know 會 for an acquired skill, as in 我會說中文. 可以 in this lesson explains an opportunity or possible benefit, not that someone has mastered a skill.
u8-possible.remember: First name the activity; then 可以 + what it enables. Keep 會 for the learned-skill meaning you already know.

examples.meaning: Watching movies can be a way to learn Chinese.
Listening to Chinese can be a way to learn Chinese.

u8-counteroffer.title: Turn a declined plan into an alternative
u8-counteroffer.pattern: 不想 + first activity；suggest another plan
u8-counteroffer.explanation: Use the language you know to negotiate a plan in small steps. 不想 declines the proposed activity. A second sentence with 一起 and 吧 offers another plan. The listener can accept with 好啊. There is no new word for “instead” here: the order of the two sentences makes the alternative clear. An opinion with 覺得 can explain why someone likes a proposal, but does not by itself confirm they will attend.
u8-counteroffer.remember: Track what is only proposed and what both people finally agree to do.

examples.text: 我不想去游泳。我們一起看電影吧。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ bù xiǎng qù yóuyǒng. Wǒmen yìqǐ kàn diànyǐng ba.
examples.meaning: I do not want to go swimming. Let’s watch a movie together.

examples.text: 好啊！我們今天一起看電影。
examples.pinyin: Hǎo a! Wǒmen jīntiān yìqǐ kàn diànyǐng.
examples.meaning: Sure! We will watch a movie together today.

u9-music.title: Listen to music
u9-music.explanation: 音樂 (yīnyuè) means music. You already know 聽, to listen: 聽音樂 means listen to music, with no extra word for English “to.” Put 喜歡 before the whole activity to say you like it. 樂 has more than one reading; in 音樂 use yuè. Learn the two characters together as this word.
u9-music.remember: 音樂 is the thing you listen to; 聽音樂 is the activity.

examples.meaning: I like listening to music.
Do you like listening to music?

u9-exercise.title: Exercise is an activity
u9-exercise.explanation: 運動 (yùndòng) means to exercise. The complete word can be the action: 我運動, I exercise. Add the familiar 常 for often, or 想 for wanting to do it. You do not need to add 做 before 運動 in these sentences. 運 and 動 work together as one activity word.
u9-exercise.remember: 常運動 describes a habit; 想運動 describes a wish.

examples.meaning: I exercise often.
I want to exercise tomorrow.

u9-frequency.title: Often, also often, or not often
u9-frequency.explanation: You know 常, often. 不常 means not often: put 不 before 常. It describes frequency, not whether you enjoy the activity. 我不常運動 does not tell us whether I like exercise. When adding “also,” put 也 first: 也常, also often, or 也不常, also not often. These words all come before the action.
u9-frequency.remember: 不常 = not often. 不喜歡 = do not like. Put 也 before 不 and 常.

examples.meaning: I do not exercise often.

examples.text: 她常聽音樂，我也常聽音樂。
examples.pinyin: Tā cháng tīng yīnyuè, wǒ yě cháng tīng yīnyuè.
examples.meaning: She often listens to music; I also often listen to music.

examples.text: 他不常運動，我也不常運動。
examples.pinyin: Tā bù cháng yùndòng, wǒ yě bù cháng yùndòng.
examples.meaning: He does not exercise often; I do not exercise often either.

u9-basketball.title: Play basketball
u9-basketball.explanation: 打籃球 (dǎ lánqiú) means play basketball. 打 means hit or play in this expression; 籃球 (lánqiú) is basketball. 籃 means basket and 球 means ball. Chinese does not use one action word for every sport, so learn each sport together with its verb. Reuse 喜歡 + activity to describe a preference, and 去 + activity to go and do it.
u9-basketball.remember: Keep the pair 打籃球: play + basketball. 籃 contains the bamboo top; 球 is the ball.

examples.meaning: I like playing basketball.
We are going to play basketball tomorrow.

u9-soccer.title: Kick the ball: play soccer
u9-soccer.explanation: 踢足球 (tī zúqiú) means play soccer, or football. 踢 means kick; 足球 (zúqiú) names the sport. 足 means foot, while 球 is the ball you learned in 籃球. Use 踢 for soccer and 打 for basketball. To say you like playing, put 喜歡 before 踢足球. To suggest going to play, reuse 我們 + 去 + activity + 吧.
u9-soccer.remember: 打籃球 uses 打; 踢足球 uses 踢. The foot component in 踢 helps you remember kicking.

examples.meaning: I like playing soccer.
Let’s go play soccer.

u9-tennis.title: One more sport: tennis
u9-tennis.explanation: 打網球 (dǎ wǎngqiú) means play tennis. 網球 (wǎngqiú) is tennis; 網 means net and 球 is the familiar ball character. Like basketball, tennis uses 打. Only 網 is a new character in this sport: reuse 打 and 球.
u9-tennis.remember: 打籃球 = play basketball; 打網球 = play tennis; 踢足球 = play soccer.

examples.meaning: I like playing tennis.

u9-choice.title: Ask someone to choose
u9-choice.pattern: 你 + 想 / 喜歡 + activity A + 還是 + activity B？
u9-choice.explanation: 還是 (háishì) means “or” in a question offering alternatives. Put it between the two activities. The shared 你想 or 你喜歡 applies to both choices. 你想打網球還是游泳？ asks which you want to do, not simply yes or no. Name the activity in your answer. For this direct choice-question pattern, do not add 嗎. If both appeal, you can say 我喜歡…，也喜歡… using the familiar 也.
u9-choice.remember: 還是 offers choices. 嗎 asks yes or no. Answer a choice question by naming your choice.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng dǎ wǎngqiú háishì yóuyǒng?
examples.meaning: Do you want to play tennis or swim?
I want to swim.

examples.text: 你喜歡聽音樂還是看電影？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ xǐhuān tīng yīnyuè háishì kàn diànyǐng?
examples.meaning: Do you like listening to music or watching movies?

u9-topic.title: Put the activity you are discussing first
u9-topic.explanation: You can begin by naming the activity you want to discuss, then say what you think about it. This first part is the topic. 我喜歡打網球 becomes 打網球，我喜歡: “As for playing tennis, I like it.” The person 我 still comes before 喜歡 in the comment. Do not add 是, 的, or a second object for English “it.” Starting with the activity makes clear what your comment is about.
u9-topic.remember: Name the topic first; then say who feels or does what. The order exercises here start with the activity.

examples.meaning: As for playing tennis, I like it.
As for listening to music, I like it a lot.

u9-both-topics.title: Talk about both activities
u9-both-topics.pattern: activity A、activity B，person + 都 + 喜歡
u9-both-topics.explanation: When you name two activities as the topic and say you like both, use 都 in the comment. Its meaning now points back to the two activities at the beginning. 打籃球、踢足球，我都喜歡 means I like both playing basketball and playing soccer. Keep 都 after 我 and before 喜歡. This lets you answer a choice question by saying both appeal to you.
u9-both-topics.remember: Two activities first; then 我都喜歡. Here 都 includes both activities, not a group of people.

examples.text: 打籃球、踢足球，我都喜歡。
examples.pinyin: Dǎ lánqiú, tī zúqiú, wǒ dōu xǐhuān.
examples.meaning: As for playing basketball and soccer, I like both.

u10-also-all.title: Another whole group does too
u10-also-all.explanation: You already know 也 adds a matching fact and 都 includes everyone in a group. Now combine them. Build the meaning from the action outward: 喜歡游泳 = like swimming; 都喜歡游泳 = all like swimming; 也都喜歡游泳 = also all like swimming. The group comes first, then 也, then 都. Use 也 when the context supplies a matching fact, often in a previous statement. These sentences describe shared preferences; they do not say everyone swims together.
u10-also-all.remember: For “also all,” keep 也 before 都. 都 includes the members of the group before it; 也 connects this fact to another relevant fact.

examples.text: 我喜歡游泳，他們也都喜歡游泳。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuān yóuyǒng, tāmen yě dōu xǐhuān yóuyǒng.
examples.meaning: I like swimming; all of them like swimming too.

examples.text: 我家人都喜歡照相，他家人也都喜歡照相。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiārén dōu xǐhuān zhàoxiàng, tā jiārén yě dōu xǐhuān zhàoxiàng.
examples.meaning: My family members all like taking photos; his family members all like taking photos too.

u10-all-often.title: Everyone has the habit
u10-all-often.explanation: 常 tells how often an action happens. 都 tells who is included. Build outward: 看電影 = watch movies; 常看電影 = often watch movies; 都常看電影 = all often watch movies. In 我們都常看電影, each of us has this habit. The sentence does not say we watch together or at the same time. Keep 都 before 常 for this meaning.
u10-all-often.remember: Read the layers: everyone in the group → often → action. 都 is about the group; 常 is about frequency.

examples.meaning: We all often watch movies.
They all often exercise.

u10-also-all-often.title: That is our habit too
u10-also-all-often.pattern: group + 也 + 都 + 常 + activity
u10-also-all-often.explanation: Add 也 to a habit shared by every member of another group. Start with 喝茶, drink tea. 常喝茶 means often drink tea. 都常喝茶 means all often drink tea. 也都常喝茶 means also all often drink tea. So the practiced order is 也 → 都 → 常 → action. First establish the matching habit in the conversation; then add the group. You are combining familiar meanings, not learning a new word for “together.”
u10-also-all-often.remember: 也 adds “too,” 都 includes everyone, and 常 adds “often.” We are practicing this order, not every possible adverb combination.

examples.text: 我常喝茶，他們也都常喝茶。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ cháng hē chá, tāmen yě dōu cháng hē chá.
examples.meaning: I often drink tea; all of them often drink tea too.

examples.text: 你常游泳，我們也都常游泳。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ cháng yóuyǒng, wǒmen yě dōu cháng yóuyǒng.
examples.meaning: You often swim; all of us often swim too.

u10-also-no-have.title: I do not have one either
u10-also-no-have.explanation: You already use 沒有 for “do not have.” Put 也 before the whole negative: 也沒有 means “do not have … either.” You can add another person with the same situation, or another thing the same person does not have. In the second example, the second 我 is understood because the person has not changed. Keep 也 before 沒有. This lesson uses 沒有 only for having something, not as a new rule about past actions.
u10-also-no-have.remember: Use 也不 with familiar verbs such as 喜歡. Use 也沒有 with 有: the negative of 有 is 沒有, never 不有.

examples.text: 他沒有哥哥，我也沒有哥哥。
examples.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu gēge, wǒ yě méiyǒu gēge.
examples.meaning: He does not have an older brother; I do not have an older brother either.

examples.text: 我沒有哥哥，也沒有姐姐。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ méiyǒu gēge, yě méiyǒu jiějie.
examples.meaning: I do not have an older brother, and I do not have an older sister either.

u10-none.title: Nobody in the group
u10-none.explanation: To say a statement is false for every member of a group, put 都 before 不. Check one person at a time. For “likes swimming”: Person 1 ❌; Person 2 ❌; Person 3 ❌. Nobody in this group likes swimming. This is 都不喜歡游泳. The order is group → 都 → 不 → 喜歡游泳: for each person, “likes swimming” is not true. We are talking about this group, not everybody in the world. Compare the two examples below with the familiar positive pattern 都喜歡.
u10-none.remember: 都不 = none of the group satisfies the statement. A dislike does not tell you whether someone knows how to do the activity.

examples.meaning: None of us likes swimming. Likes swimming: Person 1 ❌ · Person 2 ❌ · Person 3 ❌.

examples.pinyin: Tāmen dōu bù xǐhuān hē kāfēi.
examples.meaning: None of them likes drinking coffee. Likes coffee: Person 1 ❌ · Person 2 ❌ · Person 3 ❌.

u10-none-have.title: Nobody has it; I have neither
u10-none-have.pattern: group or topic set + … + 都 + 沒有 + …
u10-none-have.explanation: 有 uses 沒有 as its negative. Add 都 before 沒有 to apply “do not have” to every member of a set. In 我們都沒有哥哥, 都 refers to us: no one in our group has an older brother. The set can also be the two topics you already learned to put first. In 哥哥、姐姐，我都沒有, it refers to older brothers and older sisters: I have neither. Read the words before 都 to find the set. Do not replace 沒有 with 不有.
u10-none-have.remember: 都沒有 can mean “none of us has …” or “I have neither,” depending on the set before it. 沒有 stays together.

examples.meaning: None of us has an older brother.
Older brothers and older sisters — I have neither.
None of them has an older sister.
Older brothers and older sisters — he has neither.

u10-not-all.title: Not everyone is the same
u10-not-all.explanation: 不都 rejects “all.” First imagine three people: Person 1 ✅ likes swimming; Person 2 ❌ does not; Person 3 ✅ likes swimming. 他們不都喜歡游泳 fits: not all of them like swimming. Contrast 都不: Person 1 ❌; Person 2 ❌; Person 3 ❌, so nobody likes it. 不都 does not tell us an exact number. At least one member does not fit the statement. In everyday group comparisons it often suggests a mixed group, like the picture here, but the words “not all” alone do not guarantee that anyone does fit. For an explicitly all-negative group, use 都不 to say “none” precisely.
u10-not-all.remember: 都不: everyone → not; none. 不都: not → everyone; not all. The two orders make different claims and are not interchangeable.

examples.meaning: Not all of them like swimming. One possible group: Person 1 ✅ · Person 2 ❌ · Person 3 ✅.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen bù dōu xǐhuān hē kāfēi.
examples.meaning: Not all of us like drinking coffee. One possible group: Person 1 ❌ · Person 2 ✅ · Person 3 ❌.

u10-morning-time.title: Say when: 早上
u10-morning-time.pattern: (day) + 早上 + subject + action OR subject + 早上 + action
u10-morning-time.explanation: 早上 means “morning” or “in the morning.” Put the time before the action it frames. If you also name a day, Chinese normally goes from the larger time to the smaller time: 明天早上, “tomorrow morning.” A time phrase may come before the subject or just after it.
u10-morning-time.remember: Time comes before the action. For two time words, go from larger to smaller: 明天 → 早上.

examples.meaning: I often drink tea in the morning.
Tomorrow morning, we are going swimming.

u10-evening-time.title: Say when: 晚上
u10-evening-time.pattern: (day) + 晚上 + subject + action OR subject + 晚上 + action
u10-evening-time.explanation: 晚上 means “evening” or “at night.” Like 早上, it comes before the action it frames. With a day, keep the larger-to-smaller order: 明天晚上, “tomorrow evening.”
u10-evening-time.remember: Put 晚上 before the action. With 明天, say 明天晚上—not 晚上明天.

examples.meaning: I often watch movies in the evening.
We are watching a movie tomorrow evening.

u10-eat-dinner.title: Eat dinner
u10-eat-dinner.explanation: 吃 is the verb “to eat.” 晚飯 is dinner, the evening meal. Put the verb first: 吃晚飯. You can place a time such as 晚上 before this action.
u10-eat-dinner.remember: Action first, meal second: 吃 + 晚飯.

examples.meaning: I eat dinner in the evening.
We eat dinner together.

u10-how-about.title: Check a suggestion with 好不好
u10-how-about.explanation: After you suggest a plan, add 好不好？ to ask whether it sounds good to the other person. It literally presents “good or not good,” but the natural meaning here is “How about it?” or “Does that sound good?” Keep it at the end of the complete suggestion.
u10-how-about.remember: Say the plan first, then ask 好不好？ for agreement.

examples.text: 我們晚上一起吃晚飯，好不好？
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen wǎnshàng yìqǐ chī wǎnfàn, hǎo bu hǎo?
examples.meaning: How about we eat dinner together this evening?

examples.text: 我們明天早上去游泳，好不好？
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen míngtiān zǎoshàng qù yóuyǒng, hǎo bu hǎo?
examples.meaning: How about we go swimming tomorrow morning?

u10-cuisine.title: Choose something to eat
u10-cuisine.pattern: 吃 + 菜; country name + 菜
u10-cuisine.explanation: 菜 can mean a dish or a cuisine. 吃菜 means to eat dishes or food. A country name before 菜 names that country’s cuisine; you will learn one in the next lesson. Keep the familiar order: person, time if needed, then 吃 and the food.
u10-cuisine.remember: 晚飯 names the meal. 菜 names dishes or a cuisine. Both follow 吃.

examples.meaning: We eat the dishes together.
I would like to eat some dishes this evening.

u10-vietnam.title: Vietnamese food
u10-vietnam.pattern: 越南 + 菜 → 越南菜
u10-vietnam.explanation: 越南, Yuènán, is Vietnam. Add the familiar 菜 to name its cuisine: 越南菜, Vietnamese food. This is a country name plus 菜, not a new verb. You can now say what kind of food you would like for dinner.
u10-vietnam.remember: 越南 = Vietnam; 越南菜 = Vietnamese food. Put 吃 before the food.

examples.meaning: I would like to eat Vietnamese food.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen wǎnshàng qù chī Yuènán cài.
examples.meaning: We are going to eat Vietnamese food this evening.

u11-cup.title: Count cups of a drink
u11-cup.explanation: 杯, bēi, counts cups of a drink. You already know number + measure word + noun. Here use 杯: 一杯茶 is one cup of tea and 兩杯茶 is two cups of tea. Keep 兩 before the measure word. At the counter, the familiar 我要 can introduce your order.
u11-cup.remember: Number → 杯 → drink. Use 兩杯 for two cups.

examples.meaning: I would like one cup of tea.
I would like two cups of coffee.

u11-hot.title: Make it hot
u11-hot.pattern: 熱 + drink; drink + 很 + 熱
u11-hot.explanation: 熱, rè, means hot. 熱茶 is hot tea and 熱咖啡 is hot coffee. For these familiar short descriptions, place 熱 directly before the drink without 的. When you describe a drink in a sentence, use the pattern you already know: 這杯茶很熱. Temperature and taste are separate: 熱 is hot; 好喝 means tastes good.
u11-hot.remember: 一杯熱茶: one + cup + hot + tea. 熱 describes temperature.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yào yì bēi rè chá.
examples.meaning: I would like a cup of hot tea.
This cup of coffee is hot.
